title: Russia and Ukraine Are Mutually Shutting Down the Black Sea
gist: Ukraine froze maritime transport at its three remaining Black Sea ports on July 23 after Russian strikes hit 57 merchant ships in a month, but unlike the 2022 blockade this is a risk-pricing collapse — war-risk premiums and force majeure, not mines — and Ukraine’s own drone campaign has idled Novorossiysk and the Kerch Strait, so the September–October harvest could trigger a 2022-scale food crisis with no alternative corridor able to absorb the lost 2.5–3.5 million tons a month.

themes.theme: Export Shutdown and Ukraine’s FX Exposure

insights.claim: Ukraine announced on July 23 that maritime transport to and from its three unoccupied Black Sea ports was effectively frozen, after Russian missile and drone attacks in July alone targeted 57 Ukrainian and foreign-flagged merchant ships in ports and at sea.
insights.speaker: Paul Hockenos
insights.so_what: A hard stop on Ukraine’s seaborne exports is the trigger to watch for wheat, corn, and sunflower oil price gaps.
insights.locator: On July 23, Ukraine announced that maritime transport

insights.claim: Three Russian missiles struck the Turkish-owned bulk carrier Golden Leo, sailing under the flag of Guinea-Bissau, in open water off Odesa on July 19, killing 10 people; the ship sank on July 27.
insights.speaker: Paul Hockenos
insights.so_what: Direct lethal strikes on third-country-flagged commercial tonnage are what closed the trade — insurers and crews, not navies, are the binding constraint.
insights.locator: Russian missile and drone attacks in July alone

insights.claim: This year’s strikes had already cut Ukraine’s grain exports by roughly a third and doubled shipping freight costs into and out of the country before the July shutdown.
insights.speaker: Paul Hockenos
insights.so_what: Freight cost doubling on Ukrainian routes flows straight into landed grain prices for import-dependent buyers in Africa and the Middle East.
insights.locator: By then, this year’s strikes had already cut

insights.claim: Ukraine’s agricultural sector faces a direct export revenue loss of between $1.5 billion and $3 billion this year, according to its agriculture minister.
insights.speaker: Paul Hockenos
insights.so_what: A multibillion-dollar hole in Ukraine’s export earnings widens the external financing gap that Western donors must cover.
insights.locator: Agricultural stocks are piling up

insights.claim: Ukraine’s Black Sea maritime corridors handle approximately 90 percent of its agricultural exports plus the lion’s share of mining and steel products, and those sectors account for three-quarters of the country’s foreign-currency earnings.
insights.speaker: Paul Hockenos
insights.so_what: Closing the Black Sea removes about three-quarters of Ukraine’s FX income at source — the hryvnia and the donor funding requirement are the transmission channel.
insights.locator: Ukraine’s Black Sea maritime corridors handle approximately

insights.claim: The current shutdown is not a physical blockade: Russia is striking ships, crews, and cargo directly rather than obstructing them, so grain isn’t moving despite an open corridor.
insights.speaker: Paul Hockenos
insights.so_what: Diplomatic corridor deals cannot fix this the way the 2022 grain initiative did — the fix has to run through insurance and risk, not navigation rights.
insights.quote: This is a market collapse driven by cost and risk, not a siege.
insights.locator: Moreover, the impediment this time around

insights.claim: War-risk premiums on freight rates and shipping insurance have spiked where cover is available at all, and ship owners are citing force majeure to walk away from charters.
insights.speaker: Paul Hockenos
insights.so_what: Force majeure invocation is the mechanism that empties the corridor; monitor Lloyd’s war-risk listings as the real-time indicator of Ukrainian export capacity.
insights.locator: War-risk premiums on freight rates and shipping insurance have spiked

insights.claim: War-risk insurance compensates for financial loss to vessel, cargo, and liability but does nothing to reduce physical risk to the crew, making it compensation rather than protection.
insights.speaker: Paul Hockenos
insights.so_what: State-backed insurance backstops can restore insurability without restoring traffic — do not model a backstop announcement as a volume recovery.
insights.locator: War-risk insurance compensates for financial loss

insights.claim: After hostilities knocked out commercial war-risk coverage in the Gulf starting in March 2026 and premiums spiked fivefold, the United States set up a $20 billion maritime reinsurance plan covering hull, cargo, war protection, and indemnity — yet most shippers are still steering clear of the Gulf.
insights.speaker: Paul Hockenos
insights.so_what: The Gulf precedent quantifies the ceiling on state reinsurance: $20 billion of capacity did not reopen the route, so expect the same for any Black Sea equivalent.
insights.locator: In the Gulf, after hostilities knocked out commercial war-risk coverage

insights.claim: The International Transport Workers’ Federation argues no vessel should transit the war zone with civilian crew aboard until safety is guaranteed, framing the strikes as deliberate acts against civilian workers rather than collateral damage.
insights.speaker: Paul Hockenos
insights.so_what: Organized labor refusal adds a second, non-financial lock on the corridor that money alone cannot unlock.
insights.quote: “These are not accidents, not collateral damage, these are deliberate acts against civilian workers who have no part in this conflict and no power to escape it.”
insights.locator: Stephen Cotton of the International Transport Workers’ Federation

themes.theme: Why Markets Haven’t Blown Out Yet

insights.claim: The 2022 crisis was severe because Ukrainian silos were full from a record harvest and roughly 20 million tons of grain ended up stranded when Russian warships and mines cordoned the Odesa coast.
insights.speaker: Paul Hockenos
insights.so_what: The 20-million-ton stranded stock is the benchmark for how big a supply shock a Black Sea closure can generate when timing is unfavorable.
insights.locator: The 2022-2023 events involved Russian warships

insights.claim: Ukraine had already shipped its recent harvest before Russia shut down the ports this time and global grain markets are relatively flush, which is why the 2026 shutdown has not yet produced 2022-style price turmoil, according to Oleg Nivievskyi of the Kyiv School of Economics.
insights.speaker: Paul Hockenos
insights.so_what: The calm is a timing artifact, not resilience — the same closure with full silos reprices grain violently.
insights.quote: “In February 2022, agricultural stocks in Ukraine were full,”
insights.locator: But this crisis, thus far, hasn’t triggered anything like

insights.claim: A new harvest arrives in September and October, and by autumn the world could face a food crisis every bit as severe as the one in 2022 if the ports remain closed.
insights.speaker: Paul Hockenos
insights.so_what: September–October is the dated catalyst — build long grain optionality into that window rather than trading the current calm.
insights.quote: “In September and October, however, there’ll be a new harvest,”
insights.locator: Global grain markets are jittery but functional for now

themes.theme: The Alternative Corridors Cannot Absorb It

insights.claim: Overland and river alternatives cannot absorb the roughly 2.5 to 3.5 million tons a month of capacity Ukraine has lost from its deepwater ports: Danube river exports currently move around 100,000 tons a month, trucks roughly another 100,000, and rail to the western border tops out at 300,000 to 400,000 tons.
insights.speaker: Paul Hockenos
insights.so_what: The arithmetic caps substitution at roughly a fifth of lost volume — the export gap is structural, not logistical.
insights.locator: Moreover, even given good will, these corridors simply can’t absorb

insights.claim: Ukraine has no viable substitute for its Black Sea ports in the longer term, and the Danube ports plus Central European roads and railways together could handle at best half of the Black Sea ports’ monthly capacity, according to Slawomir Matuszak of the Warsaw-based Center for Eastern Studies.
insights.speaker: Paul Hockenos
insights.so_what: Any recovery scenario for Ukrainian exports requires the sea lanes reopening; overland investment is a partial hedge at best.
insights.quote: “In the longer term, Ukraine has no viable substitute for its Black Sea ports,”
insights.locator: “In the longer term, Ukraine has no viable substitute

insights.claim: Alternative routes would cost Ukrainian exporters an additional $45 to $50 per ton, according to Reuters.
insights.speaker: Paul Hockenos
insights.so_what: A $45–50 per ton logistics penalty compresses Ukrainian farmgate prices and erodes competitiveness versus Russian and South American grain.
insights.locator: the alternative routes would cost Ukrainian exporters

insights.claim: Shifting load to Danube routes depends on water levels rising from their current historic lows in the autumn, adding a physical constraint on top of the political one.
insights.speaker: Paul Hockenos
insights.so_what: Low Danube water levels mean the fallback route is weakest precisely when harvest volume peaks.
insights.locator: Some of the load can be shifted to Danube River routes

insights.claim: The 2022–23 EU rescue via Danube ports and Central European rail triggered farmer protests in Poland, Hungary, and Slovakia and national embargoes on Ukrainian agricultural goods despite EU policy, and this time there is no discussion of completely reopening EU markets.
insights.speaker: Paul Hockenos
insights.so_what: The political capacity for a Central European bailout of Ukrainian exports is exhausted — assume the 2022 workaround is not repeatable.
insights.locator: The European Union came to Ukraine’s rescue

insights.claim: Ukraine appealed to the U.N. on July 27 to facilitate safe Black Sea transit, accusing Russia of war crimes and economic terror and comparing the disruption to energy-route disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.
insights.speaker: Paul Hockenos
insights.so_what: Ukraine is explicitly bidding for a repeat of the 2022 Black Sea Grain Initiative; a U.N. deal would be the fastest bearish catalyst for grain prices.
insights.locator: This is why Ukraine urged the United Nations on July 27

themes.theme: Ukraine’s Mirror Campaign Against Russian Exports

insights.claim: Russia halted Kerch Strait transit on July 10 after Ukrainian one-way aerial and maritime drones hit more than 100 vessels in the Sea of Azov area, and exported just 1.8 million metric tons of wheat in July — a collapse versus the same month in 2025.
insights.speaker: Paul Hockenos
insights.so_what: Both Black Sea exporters are now impaired simultaneously, which removes the usual substitution buffer that kept 2022 from becoming famine.
insights.locator: The picture is further complicated by Ukraine’s own strikes

insights.claim: Novorossiysk, Russia’s busiest seaport on the Black Sea’s northeast coast, is virtually idle as a result of Ukrainian drone strikes.
insights.speaker: Paul Hockenos
insights.so_what: Novorossiysk handles Russian grain and energy flows — its idling is a bullish supply shock beyond agriculture.
insights.locator: Russia’s busiest seaport—Novorossiysk

insights.claim: Ukraine is straining global grain supplies through its own strikes on Russian shipping even as it asks the U.N. to force Russia to stand down on humanitarian grounds — a contradiction Kyiv did not acknowledge in New York.
insights.speaker: Paul Hockenos
insights.so_what: The humanitarian framing is unlikely to secure a one-sided U.N. remedy; any deal will have to be reciprocal, which lengthens the timeline.
insights.locator: Ukraine may be inflicting economic damage on Russia

insights.claim: Russia’s main grain lobby group complained on July 31 that Ukrainian strikes on its transports could result in hunger in Africa and the Middle East, mirroring the argument Kyiv makes against Moscow.
insights.speaker: Paul Hockenos
insights.so_what: Both sides now invoke third-world hunger, signaling that food-security leverage has become an explicit weapon on both sides of the war.
insights.locator: Russia’s main grain lobby group complained on July 31
